**Surah al-A'la (The Most High)**

Meccan, and its verses number nineteen.

﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High.﴾ That is: declare your Lord, mighty and majestic, free from *ilhad* (deviation, i.e., distorting the meaning of His name) through corrupt *ta'wilat* (interpretations, i.e., deviant readings); free from applying His name to anything other than Him in a way that suggests they share it; and free from mentioning it without due reverence and veneration. "Al-A'la" (the Most High) is either an attribute of "Lord," which is the more apparent reading, or an attribute of "name." It has also been read as "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High." In a hadith, when ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Place it in your bowing." Then when ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ was revealed, he said: "Place it in your prostration." They used to say in bowing, "O Allah, to You I have bowed," and in prostration, "O Allah, to You I have prostrated."

The relative pronoun ﴿الَّذِي﴾ ("who") is an additional attribute (ṣifah) of "the Lord" (lil-Rabb) according to the first grammatical reading, and it is in the accusative case as an expression of praise (madḥ) according to the second reading; this is so that there is no separation between the described noun and its attribute by means of another's attribute. That is: He created everything and then made its creation proportionate (fa-sawwā), by granting it that by which its perfection is attained and its livelihood is made possible.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 87, verse 3:

And His saying, ﴿Who measured and then guided﴾: either it is another attribute of "the Lord," like the first relative clause, or it is coordinated with it (ma'tuf 'alayhi). The same applies to what follows it: He measured (qaddara) the kinds of things, their types, their individuals, their quantities, their attributes, their actions, and their terms (ajal).

﴿Then guided﴾, that is: He directed each one of them to that from which it proceeds and which befits it, by nature (tab') or by choice (ikhtiyar). He facilitated for it what it was created for, by creating inclinations (muyul) and inspirations (ilhamat), by establishing signs (dala'il) and sending down revelations (ayat). If you were to examine the conditions of plants and animals, you would see in each of them what minds are bewildered by. It is related that when a viper (af'a) reaches a thousand years of age, it goes blind, and God Most High has inspired it to rub its eye with fresh fennel (raziyanj) leaves, by which its sight is returned to it. Thus, when blindness comes upon it, it may be in a desert at a great distance from the inhabited land, yet it will traverse that distance until it attacks some orchards and finds a fennel plant without fail, rubs its eye with its leaves, and returns seeing, by the permission of God, Mighty and Majestic. It is also related that the crocodile (timsah) has no posterior opening; rather, it expels the residue of what it eats from its mouth. God has appointed for it a bird whose sustenance is determined from that residue. When the crocodile sees the bird, it opens its mouth, and the bird enters it and eats what is in it. God Most High has created for the bird two horns, one above and one below its beak, so that the crocodile cannot close its mouth upon it. As for the varieties of His guidance, glory be to Him and exalted, to humanity in terms of the physical body, in terms of animality, and especially in terms of humanity, these are beyond what the sphere of expression and description can encompass, and none knows them except the All-Knowing, the All-Aware.
﴿And He who brings forth the pasture﴾ — i.e., who causes to grow that which cattle graze upon, fresh and tender, verdant.

﴿So He made it﴾ after that.

﴿Debris, dark-hued﴾, that is, dry, black stalks. It was also said that "أحْوى" (aḥwā, dark-green to blackish) is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of "المرعى" (al-mar'ā, the pasture), meaning: He brought it forth dark-green from the intensity of its greenness and freshness, then after that made it debris.

The Almighty's saying, ﴿We shall make you recite, so you will not forget﴾, is an explanation of God Most High's special guidance to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), following the explanation of His general guidance to all His creatures. This special guidance is the Prophet's (peace and blessings be upon him) guidance to receive the revelation and to memorize the Qur'an, which is "a guidance for the worlds," and his (peace and blessings be upon him) success in guiding all people.

The sin (sīn) in "sanuqri'uka" is either for emphasis (ta'kid), or it is because what is meant is the making him recite what God revealed to him at that time and what will be revealed to him afterward. Thus it is a gracious promise of the continuation of revelation within the promise of recitation, meaning: We shall make you recite what We reveal to you now and hereafter through the tongue of Jibril (peace be upon him). Or: We shall make you a reciter by inspiring recitation, so you will not forget at all, in strength of memory and mastery, even though you are unlettered, not knowing what the Book is or what reading is, so that this will be another sign for you, along with what is within the midst of the clear verses you recite in terms of their inimitability and in terms of their reporting of unseen matters.

It has also been said that "fa-la tansā" is a prohibition, and the alif is for maintaining the rhyme (fāṣila), as in His saying, Most High: ﴿fa-aḍallūnā al-sabīlā﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 87, verse 7:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Except what Allah wills﴾ is an exception of the type "mufarragh" (the exception from an unstated general object) from the most general of the objects, meaning: you will not forget anything of what you recite, except what Allah wills that you forget forever, by abrogating its recitation. The turn to the noble Name (Allah) is for the cultivation of awe and for announcing that the will revolves around the title of divinity (uluhiyya), which entails all the other attributes. It has also been said: what is meant by it is forgetting in general, but rarely and infrequently, as it is narrated that "he, upon him be prayer and peace, dropped a verse in his recitation during the prayer, so Ubayy thought that it had been abrogated, and he asked him, and he, upon him be prayer and peace, said: 'I forgot it.'" (p-145) It has also been said: it is the negation of forgetting altogether, for rarity may be used in the sense of negation. So what is meant by forgetting then is forgetting in its totality, since that is what is negated entirely, not what one may forget and then remember.

﴿Indeed He knows what is manifest and what is hidden﴾ is a causal justification for what precedes it, meaning: He knows what has appeared and what is concealed of matters, among which is what has been revealed to you, so He causes to forget whatever He wills to cause forgetting, and preserves in memory whatever He wills to preserve, because of the benefits for your religion attached to each of these.

﴿And We will ease you toward ease.﴾ It is coordinated (ʿatf) with "We will teach you to recite (nuqriʾuka)," as the shift (iltifat) to the narrative (ḥikayah) indicates. What lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ) that comes in for the reason mentioned, which is the justification. Making the facilitation contingent on it (ʿalayhi al-salatu wa al-salam) is notable, since the common practice is to make it contingent on matters that are subjected to the agent, as in His saying: ﴿And ease for me my affair﴾. This indicates the great extent of his (ʿalayhi al-salatu wa al-salam) empowerment over ease and his mastery of it, to the point that it became a firmly established disposition (malakah rasikhah) for him, as though he (ʿalayhi al-salatu wa al-salam) was created with it. This is like the statement of the Prophet (ʿalayhi al-salatu wa al-salam): "Act, for each is made easy for that for which he was created." That is, We will grant you continuous success (tawfiq mustamirr) in the easy way in every chapter of the religion, in knowledge and in teaching, in guidance and in giving guidance. Thus included in it is the facilitation of the way of receiving revelation and of comprehending what it contains of the rulings of the tolerant Law (al-shariʿah al-samhah) and the divine ordinances (al-nawamis al-ilahiyyah), of what pertains to perfecting his own soul (ʿalayhi al-salatu wa al-salam) and perfecting others, as the particle "fa" (fa'), in His saying, the Exalted, makes clear:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 87, verse 9:

﴿So remind, if the reminder benefits.﴾ That is: remind the people according to what We have made easy for you, by means of what is revealed to you, and guide them to what is in its contents of the legal rulings (ahkam shar'iyyah, the rulings of the Divine Law), as you used to do, not after the matter had become firmly established for you, as has been said. The restriction of the reminding to the benefit of the reminder (naf' al-dhikra) is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would often remind them, exerting the utmost effort in it and exceeding every known limit in earnestness, out of eagerness for their faith; yet it only increased some of them in disbelief and obstinacy. So he (peace and blessings be upon him) was commanded to confine the reminding to the materials of benefit in general, by making those he reminds, wholly or partly, those from whom remembrance is hoped for, and not to exhaust himself in reminding those whom the reminder brings only arrogance and aversion, namely those whose hearts are sealed. This is as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾, and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So turn away from him who turns away from Our remembrance﴾. And it has been said: it is a censure of the reminders, and a report about their state, and a suggestion that the reminder would have an effect on them, and a recording against them of being sealed upon their hearts, like your saying to the preacher: "Admonish the tax-collectors, if they hear from you"—intending that it is something that will not happen. The first is more fitting to His saying, Exalted is He: *

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 87, verse 10:

﴿Whoever fears will be reminded.﴾ That is: whoever is of a nature that fears God, exalted is He, with its true fear will be reminded by your reminding, or whoever fears God, exalted is He, in general, and that increases by the reminder, so he reflects upon some matter he was reminded of, and thus he becomes certain of its truth and believes in it. It has been said: "in" (in) is in the sense of "when" (idh), as in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And you will be the superior ones if you are believers﴾, that is: since you are believers. It has been said: it is in the sense of "what" (ma), that is: remind with what the reminder benefits, for it is never free of benefit in any case. It has been said: there is an omitted element, and the estimate is: "whether the reminder benefits or whether it does not benefit," as in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Garments that protect you from the heat﴾. This was said by al-Farra', al-Nahhas, al-Jurjani and al-Zahrawi.

﴿And there will avoid it﴾, i.e., the reminder.

﴿The most wretched﴾ among the disbelievers, because of his extreme enmity toward the Prophet (ﷺ). It is also said that it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and Utba ibn Abi Rabi'a.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 87, verse 12:**

﴿who shall burn in the greatest Fire﴾. That is, the lowest of the levels of the Fire. It has also been said: the greatest (al-Kubra) is the Fire of Jahannam (Hell), and the lesser (al-Sughra) is the fire of this world, because of the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Your fire is one part of seventy parts of the fire of Jahannam."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 87, verse 13:

﴿Then he will neither die therein﴾, so as to find rest.

﴿Nor will he live﴾ a life that benefits him. And "thumma" (then) here indicates remoteness in the degrees of severity, because the oscillation between death and life is more dreadful than the burning.

﴿Qad aflaḥa﴾ (Indeed, he has succeeded): that is, he was saved from what is disliked and attained what he hoped for.

﴿man tazakkā﴾ (who purifies himself): that is, he was purified from disbelief and sins by remembering and being admonished by the reminder; or, he increases in piety and fear [of God], from al-zakāʾ (purification), which is growth (al-namāʾ). It was also said: he purified himself for the prayer. And it was said: tazakkā is taffaʿala from al-zakāh (almsgiving). The word "qad" (indeed) is used because, when the report of the bad state of the one who turns away from the reminder in the Hereafter is given, the listener expects and awaits the report of the good state of the one who remembers in it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 87, verse 15:

﴿And he remembers the name of his Lord﴾ with his heart and his tongue.

﴿And prays﴾ he establishes the five prayers, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And establish the prayer for My remembrance﴾. Or he says the opening takbir (takbir al-iftitah) and then prays. It is also said: "he purifies himself" (tazakka), i.e., he gives the charity of breaking the fast (sadaqat al-fitr). And "and remembers the name of his Lord" means he glorifies Him (kabbarahu) on the day of the Eid, and then prays, i.e., his prayer.

**Bal tu'thiruna al-hayah al-dunya** ("Rather, you prefer the worldly life") is an *idrab* (a turning away from a previous statement, an abrupt shift) from an implied element that the discourse leads to, as if it had been said right after the explanation of what leads to success: "You do not do that; rather, you prefer the fleeting, hastening pleasures, so you strive to obtain them." The address is either to the disbelievers, in which case preferring the worldly life means being content with it, feeling secure in it, and turning away from the Hereafter entirely, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who do not expect to meet Us, and are content with the life of this world and feel secure in it﴾ (the verse). Or the address is to everyone, in which case preferring it means something more general than what was mentioned, which a person almost always cannot avoid: giving precedence to the side of this world over the Hereafter in one's striving and in the ordering of one's priorities. The *iltifat* (a shift from one grammatical person to another) according to the first view serves to intensify the rebuke, and according to the second view it does so as well with respect to the disbelievers, and serves to intensify the reproach with respect to the Muslims. It was also read *yu'thirun* with the letter *ya'* (the third person).

This is the commentary on the words of Allah, "But the Hereafter is better and more enduring" (Q. 87:17). It is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to the subject of "you prefer" (tu'thirun), serving to reinforce the rebuke and reproach. That is, you prefer it over the Hereafter, while the reality is that the Hereafter is better in itself, because its bliss, although of the utmost pleasure, is pure, free from any admixture of harm, and everlasting, with no cessation to it. The omission of explaining how the bliss of this world is clouded by troubles and cut off after a short while is because this is so evident.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 87, verse 18:

﴿Indeed, this﴾ is a reference to what was mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He has certainly succeeded who purifies himself﴾. It has also been said: it refers to the whole of the surah.

﴿Is in the former scriptures﴾, meaning: its meaning is established in them.

﴿The scriptures of Abraham and Moses﴾ is a *badal* (substitute, i.e., an apposition) for "the former scriptures." That it is first left indefinite and described as "of old," and then specified and explained, magnifies its status in a way that is not hidden.

It is narrated that the total of all the books God, Mighty and Majestic, sent down is one hundred and four: He sent down ten scrolls to Adam, peace be upon him; fifty scrolls to Shith (Seth); thirty scrolls to Idris (Enoch); and ten scrolls to Ibrahim (Abraham), peace be upon them all; and the Tawrah (Torah), the Injil (Gospel), the Zabur (Psalms), and the Furqan.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-A'la, God, Exalted is He, will give him ten good deeds for every letter that God sent down to Ibrahim, Musa and Muhammad, peace be upon them."
